reader.title: Attempted lynching of Frank B. Mason
bases: A mob took a theft suspect out of a jail and hanged him three times to force a confession and threatened to shoot him, but he survived, so this was an attempted lynching (A1, A5).
Mason survived being hanged three times by a 'mob' that acted without lawful authority to make him confess to a theft, so no one was killed; the size of the mob is not given (A1, A5).

Every report is a reprint of one Ohio State Journal interview resting on Mason's own account, which a Deputy Cherrington is said to have confirmed; no independent or local West Virginia report was found (A1, A2, A5).

summary.text: The attempted lynching of Frank B. Mason took place in West Virginia some time before November 1888, when a mob took Mason, a theft suspect, out of a jail and hanged him three times to make him confess.
Mason survived, and his account reached readers through an Ohio State Journal interview that papers in three states reprinted.
Mason was a paroled prisoner who had been sent up from Noble county for seven years for burglary.
Suspected of stealing $43 from a store in Calhoun county, he was captured in Roane county by a "posse" of horsemen who leveled their guns on him as he entered a cornfield.
According to Mason, he was taken out of the jail at dusk to a beech tree about fifty rods away, where the men threw a rope over a limb and swung him off.
After the third time they let him down, they flourished revolvers in his face and threatened to shoot him and "not let his friends cut him down again."
He was then bound and taken five miles in the rain, and the wet ropes left bruises over his body and arms.
Mason was later brought from West Virginia by a Mr. Cherrington, a deputy who was reported to have confirmed his statement.
No report of arrests or prosecution of the mob appears in the coverage.
The only story found is the Ohio State Journal interview, held with penitentiary prisoners who had been hanged and survived.
Its subhead, "A Man Who Was Almost Lynched Tells How He Felt," treated the case as a curiosity about the sensations of hanging, though the text called his treatment "inhuman."
The Wood County Reporter in Wisconsin ran it on November 15, the Sully County Watchman in Dakota on November 24, and the Wheeling Sunday Register on December 9.
Its opening "It will be remembered" suggests the hanging had been reported earlier, but no such report was found.
No paper gave Mason's race, and the reprints differ only on his parole date (April 29 or 28, 1888) and the deputy's spelling ("Cheerington" or "Cherrington").

accounts.label: Mason's own account (Ohio State Journal interview)
accounts.gist: Taken from the jail at dusk, he was swung off a beech limb three times, threatened with revolvers, and then bound and carried five miles in the rain; he thought he would be hanged whether or not he confessed.

accounts.label: Deputy Cherrington
accounts.gist: Reported only as having confirmed Mason's statement about his treatment in West Virginia.

framing.detail: The Ohio State Journal story called his treatment 'inhuman' enough to 'make a Hercules shudder', but led with the curiosity of how hanging felt ('A Man Who Was Almost Lynched Tells How He Felt').
Papers in Wisconsin, Dakota and West Virginia ran the story verbatim with its credit line to the Ohio State Journal.

conflicts.note: The same story in reprint; probably a typesetting difference. The Dakota reprint (A2) also has April 29.
Spelling difference between reprints of the same story; the Dakota reprint (A2) also has 'Cheerington'.
